findings.claim: MessagePack attributes on T are ignored. When no SurrogateType is given, `Collect` always calls `CreateContractlessMembers`, which builds name-sorted string keys, and never looks at `[MessagePackObject]`/`[Key]`/`[IgnoreMember]` on T. The acceptance criterion says: 'If T does carry MessagePack attributes, they are honoured.' Ledger L24 says to follow the requirement. A referenced type declared `[MessagePackObject] class MyType { [Key(0)] int Id; [Key(1)] string Name; }` therefore gets a string-keyed map formatter instead of the int-keyed array contract it declares. Its wire format also disagrees with the defining assembly's own formatter.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.GeneratedFormatterHonoursAttributesTests.ReferencedTypeWithIntKeys_GeneratesArrayFormatter. Project A declares [MessagePackObject] with [Key(0)]/[Key(1)]. The generated MyTypeFormatter should contain WriteArrayHeader, but on head it contains only WriteMapHeader.

findings.claim: `[DataContract]`/`[DataMember]` on T are also ignored. The requirement (from the maintainer comment) says contractless mode applies only 'without [DataContract] or [MessagePackObject] on T'. A T annotated with `[DataContract]` should use its `[DataMember]` Order/Name keys and exclude unannotated members. The change serializes every public read-write member under its CLR name instead.

receipt_plan.detail: Build Project A (framework refs only) with `[DataContract] public class MyType { [DataMember(Order = 0)] public int Id {get;set;} public string Extra {get;set;} }`. Run the generator on Project B with `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] partial class MyTypeFormatter : IMessagePackFormatter<ProjectA.MyType>;`. Assert the generated formatter writes an array header and does not reference `Extra`. On head it writes a map that includes Extra.

findings.claim: Unrelated runtime change corrupts Timestamp encoding. The timestamp32 guard was changed from `(data64 & 0xffffffff00000000L) == 0` to `(data64 & 0x00000000ffffffffL) == 0`. Two effects: (1) a DateTime whose seconds' low 32 bits are zero but which has nanoseconds (e.g. 1970-01-01T00:00:00.5Z) is written as a 4-byte timestamp32 and loses its sub-second part on round trip; (2) every whole-second DateTime (e.g. 2020-01-01Z) is now written as timestamp64 instead of timestamp32, which changes the wire bytes. The requirement asks for nothing in the serializer runtime, so this contradicts 'nothing that contradicts it' and is data corruption.

receipt_plan.detail: With base-built and head-built MessagePack, run MessagePackSerializer.Serialize(new DateTime(1970,1,1,0,0,0,500,DateTimeKind.Utc)) and Serialize(new DateTime(2020,1,1,0,0,0,DateTimeKind.Utc)), then compare bytes. Base gives d7 ff ... (timestamp64) and d6 ff ... (timestamp32). Head gives d6 ff 00 00 00 00 for the first value, which deserializes to the epoch without the 500 ms, and d7 ff ... for the second.
